600 lbf Nitrous/HTPB
Hybrid Rocket Motor

Hybrid Rocket Engine Lead · Rocket Project at UCLA · 2025–2026

Flight day — successful 13,300 ft apogee with full recovery

Led end-to-end development of four SRAD 600 lbf Nitrous/HTPB hybrid rocket motors from initial concept through qualification testing and flight. The program culminated in a successful 13,300 ft apogee flight with full recovery.

As Engine Lead, I owned the full system: combustion chamber design, injector development, nozzle selection, structural analysis, test planning, anomaly investigation, and the PDR/CDR review process with industry professionals.

Chamber Pressure450 psi
Apogee13,300 ft

Key Contributions

  • Mitigated critical combustion instabilities through iterative motor geometry optimization, achieving significant dry-mass reduction
  • Conducted rigorous structural, fastener, and pressure vessel analyses on combustion chamber, injector plate, and nozzle retainment assembly using FEA and classical hand calculations
  • Fabricated flight and test hardware to precision tolerances using manual lathes, mills, and CNC machinery across Al 6061-T6, isomolded graphite, and paper phenolic ablatives
  • Spearheaded data-driven post-test anomaly investigations on static fires, resolving a major system anomaly to ensure flight readiness
  • Utilized CEA to numerically simulate steady-state combustion, informing thermal management and performance baselines
  • Authored and presented comprehensive PDR/CDR reviews to peer panels and aerospace industry professionals

Graphite Nozzle &
Nozzle Retainment System

Design Lead · Rocket Project at UCLA · 2026

Designed and manufactured a new lightweight isomolded graphite nozzle and aluminum retaining ring to replace a legacy system that suffered from repeated exhaust gas sealing failures and excessive mass. The redesign cut system mass by 33% and eliminated the sealing issue entirely.

Thermal-structural analysis was central: nozzle throat temperatures exceed 3,000°F during operation, creating severe thermal gradients that drive shear and fracture at the nozzle-retainer interface. FEA and closed-form calculations verified adequate structural margins before test.

Mass Reduction33%
Thrust Qualified635 lbf
Chamber Pressure450 psi
Nozzle MaterialIsomolded Graphite
Retainer MaterialAl 6061-T6
Analysis ToolsANSYS + Hand Calc
Isomolded graphite nozzle — post static fire, showing ablative erosion pattern
ANSYS Mechanical — maximum principal stress analysis under thermal-mechanical loading (637 psi max)

Key Contributions

  • Designed isomolded graphite nozzle geometry optimized for performance (expansion ratio) and manufacturability
  • Analyzed thermal-induced shear and fracture modes using FEA and closed-form calculations to ensure structural margins under extreme thermal gradients
  • Resolved historical exhaust gas sealing failures through new retainer interface design and O-ring groove geometry
  • Qualified new system through successful static-fire and flight tests up to 635 lbf thrust and 450 psi chamber pressure
SimulationMATLABCombustion

HTPB Fuel Grain
Regression Rate Model

Individual Project · 2026

Developed a transient, multi-dimensional MATLAB simulation to predict HTPB fuel grain regression rates in hybrid rocket motors. Grounded in empirical boundary-layer combustion theory, the model resolves the coupled 2D spatial and temporal evolution of the fuel port geometry throughout a burn.

The simulation predicted regression rates within 10% of static-fire data — accurate enough to meaningfully inform motor design decisions including fuel grain sizing, O/F ratio evolution, and burn time prediction.

Prediction AccuracyWithin 10%
Model TypeTransient 2D
FuelHTPB
PlatformMATLAB
Theory BaseBoundary-layer combustion
ValidationStatic-fire data
Regression rate (m/s) vs. axial location and time — 3D surface plot
Fuel surface temperature (K) vs. axial location and time — 3D surface plot

Technical Approach

  • Implemented advanced numerical discretization and iterative solver techniques to resolve the coupled 2D spatial and temporal evolution of the fuel port geometry
  • Applied fundamental principles of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, and convective heat transfer to accurately model the gas-surface interface and regression mechanics
  • Validated model against multiple static-fire datasets, achieving sub-10% error across varying oxidizer mass flux conditions
  • Model outputs used to directly inform motor geometry decisions for the 2026 flight campaign

Background

ABOUT

I'm a first-year Aerospace Engineering student at UCLA with a 4.0 GPA, and I build rocket engines.

As Hybrid Rocket Engine Lead at UCLA's Rocket Project, I led the full development cycle of four SRAD 600 lbf Nitrous/HTPB hybrid motors — from combustion theory and design, through machining and assembly, to static fire qualification and a successful 13,300 ft flight.

My work sits at the intersection of propulsion, structural mechanics, and hands-on manufacturing. I'm equally comfortable running ANSYS FEA simulations and standing in the machine shop turning graphite nozzles on a manual lathe.

My interests lie in propulsion, structural mechanics, and test engineering.
